title.value: F OOL SHAP WITH STEALTHILY BIASED SAMPLING
title.justification: The paper outlines a novel method for manipulating SHAP explanations using biased sampling to produce deceptive fairness evidence, referred to as "Fool SHAP," which is a central concept throughout the study.
title.quote: F OOL SHAP WITH S TEALTHILY B IASED S AMPLING.

extractions.description: The paper explores a method to manipulate SHAP explanations, which are used to identify feature contributions in machine learning models, by stealthily biased sampling of data. This manipulation can make unfair models appear fair by adjusting feature attribution, particularly during fairness audits.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The paper primarily focuses on the integrity and manipulation of machine learning explanations in fairness audits, without a direct emphasis on sustainable development.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: As Machine Learning (ML) gets more and more ubiquitous in high-stake decision contexts (e.g. , healthcare, finance, and justice), concerns about its potential to lead to discriminatory models are becoming prominent.

primary_category.justification: The content of the paper does not align with any specific Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development category, as it is primarily concerned with auditing fairness in machine learning models rather than environmental sustainability.
primary_category.quote: Our contributions can be summarized as follows: Theoretically, we formalize a notion of foreground distribution that can be used to extend Local Shapley Values (LSV) to Global Shapley Values (GSV), which can be used to decompose fairness metrics among the features.

secondary_categories.justification: Similar to the primary category, the content regarding manipulation of SHAP explanations is not directly aligned with any secondary Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development themes.
secondary_categories.quote: The first step of the attack (line 3 of Algorithm 3) requires that the company run SHAP on their own and compute the necessary coefficients to run Algorithm 1.

primary_sub_category.justification: The sub-categories are more specific subsets within primary categories, and since the primary category is N/A, this sub-category remains the same due to the paper's focus on ML fairness.
primary_sub_category.quote: These results highlight the manipulability of SHAP explanations and encourage auditors to treat them with skepticism.

secondary_sub_categories.justification: All secondary sub-categories are non-applicable as the paper does not directly contribute to or discuss Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development functionalities.
secondary_sub_categories.quote: In our experiments, we considered gender as a sensitive attribute for the Adult-Income dataset and we showed that one can diminish the attribution of this feature.

applications.justification: The paper does not detail any applications related to Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development; its applications are centered around machine learning fairness audits and feature attribution manipulation.
applications.quote: The focus of this study is on manipulating the feature attributions so that the dependence on sensitive features is hidden and the audits are misled as if the model is fair even if it is not the case.

new_primary_category.justification: Since the existing categories don't encapsulate the paper's focus, 'Machine Learning Fairness Auditing' can serve as a new category reflecting its core theme of ensuring integrity and fairness in ML models.
new_primary_category.quote: The use of auditing toolkits (Adebayo et al., 2016; Saleiro et al., 2018; Bellamy et al., 2018) is getting popular to circumvent the use of unfair models.

new_primary_sub_category.justification: The paper deals extensively with the manipulation of SHAP explanations, indicating a potential new sub-category under Machine Learning Fairness Auditing for specificity.
new_primary_sub_category.quote: In our study, we leverage the idea of stealthily biased sampling introduced by Fukuchi et al. (2020) to cherry-pick which data points to be included in the benchmark.
